summary: Defines how to run IP and ARP over an ATM network set up as a logical IP subnet. IP addresses are mapped to ATM addresses through a server. It replaces RFC 1577 and RFC 1626.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines how Internet Protocol (IP) traffic and address lookups work over an Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) network. It groups connected hosts into a logical subnet and explains how to find the ATM address for an IP address.

subtitle: How IP hosts in an ATM network form a logical subnet and resolve IP addresses to ATM addresses.

tldr.problem: IP hosts need to send datagrams across ATM virtual connections while still using IP addresses to identify other hosts.
tldr.mechanism: Hosts are grouped into a Logical IP Subnetwork, carry IP over AAL5 with LLC/SNAP, and use ATMARP and InATMARP to map IP and ATM addresses.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2225 replaces RFC 1577 and RFC 1626, leaves broadcast and multicast mappings for future work, and is updated by RFC 5494.

today: RFC 2225 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1577 and RFC 1626. It is updated by RFC 5494.

sections.title: The Classical IP-over-ATM Model
sections.content:
RFC 2225 defines how to carry IP datagrams and ATMARP messages over ATM Adaptation Layer 5 (AAL5). It treats an ATM adapter as a network interface that replaces the links between IP hosts and routers in a classical LAN model. It does not define globally connected ATM operation, MAC-level bridging, or LAN emulation.

Each administrative group configures a Logical IP Subnetwork (LIS). Members in one LIS share an IP subnet and communicate over virtual connections; traffic to another subnet goes through an IP router, even if a direct ATM connection could be made.
sections.plainLanguage: The classical model lets IP use an ATM interface much like it uses a LAN interface. Hosts in one logical subnet communicate directly, while a router connects different subnets.

sections.title: LIS Membership and Address Resolution
sections.content:
Every LIS member has the same IP network or subnet number and address mask, is attached to the ATM network, and can communicate with every other member in the LIS. With switched virtual connections (SVCs), members use ATMARP to resolve IP addresses to ATM addresses and InATMARP for reverse lookups. With permanent virtual connections (PVCs), InATMARP maps a virtual connection to an IP address.

A LIS using SVCs has one ATMARP service available to its members. A station holds its own ATM address and the configured address list for the service. A PVC-only member uses a null server list and does not query an address-resolution server.
sections.plainLanguage: A LIS is a group of ATM-connected hosts that share an IP subnet. ATMARP helps a host find the ATM address for an IP address when it needs to open a switched connection.

sections.title: Encapsulation and MTU
sections.content:
Implementations must support IEEE 802.2 LLC/SNAP encapsulation for IP datagrams; other encapsulations may be used by prior agreement or negotiation. ATM carries data in 53-octet cells, with a 5-octet header and 48 octets of data. AAL5 preserves cell order on a virtual connection but provides non-assured data transfer, so higher protocols handle retransmission.

The default IP MTU over AAL5 is 9180 octets. SVC endpoints negotiate the maximum AAL5 packet size during connection setup; forward and backward values may differ. Routers must implement Path MTU Discovery, and hosts should implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet Protocol (IP) packets are carried over Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM), with a default maximum packet size of 9180 octets. Endpoints using a switched connection can negotiate different limits for each direction.

sections.title: ATMARP Server and Client Operation
sections.content:
For SVCs, the client opens an LLC/SNAP virtual connection to the ATMARP server; the server does not open connections. A client registers an IP address by sending an ATMARP request to the server with its own IP address as the target. It must refresh its registration at least every 15 minutes.

The server learns client address mappings from requests. A request for a different target address is answered from the server table, or with an ATMARP_NAK if there is no entry. If a different ATM address already uses the same IP address on another open connection, the server reports a duplicate and does not replace the existing entry. Server entries expire after 20 minutes without refresh.

Clients also maintain local tables. A client entry is valid for at most 15 minutes and must be revalidated before traffic is sent on an open virtual connection after it ages.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients register their address with the ATMARP server and refresh it regularly. The server answers lookups from its table and flags a conflicting address instead of silently replacing it.

sections.title: ATMARP Packet Format
sections.content:
ATMARP and InATMARP packets keep the hardware type, protocol type, and operation fields in the same positions as ARP, but the remaining fields differ and the packet length varies. The ATM hardware type is 19 (0x0013), and the IP protocol type is 0x0800. Operation values identify requests, replies, inverse requests, inverse replies, and negative replies.

Address fields use type-and-length bytes. A zero length indicates a null or unknown address and allocates no address bytes. ATMARP and InATMARP messages travel inside AAL5 with an 8-octet LLC/SNAP header.
sections.plainLanguage: The address-resolution messages include fields for the source and target IP and ATM addresses. Length values let the packet omit an address that is unknown.

sections.title: Broadcast, Multicast, and Security Limits
sections.content:
ATM has no broadcast-address service or direct IP multicast mapping in this model. Members must still process received IP broadcast and subnet-broadcast datagrams as addressed to them. The RFC leaves native ATM broadcast and multicast capabilities to future work.

The RFC adds no special authentication for ATMARP and notes that unauthenticated address-resolution packets could introduce corrupt information into a server. It also identifies automatic ATM address configuration as an open issue.
sections.plainLanguage: This model does not provide ATM broadcast or multicast mappings. ATMARP packets are not authenticated, which the RFC identifies as a security weakness.
